{{Short description|Statement in information theory}}
[[FILE:Josiah Willard Gibbs -from MMS-.jpg|thumb|200px|Josiah Willard Gibbs]]
In [[information theory]], '''Gibbs' inequality''' is a statement about the [[entropy (information theory)|information entropy]] of a discrete [[probability distribution]]. Several other bounds on the entropy of probability distributions are derived from Gibbs' inequality, including [[Fano's inequality]].
It was first presented by [[J. Willard Gibbs]] in the 19th century.

==Gibbs' inequality==
Suppose that <math> P = \{ p_1 , \ldots , p_n \} </math> and <math> Q = \{ q_1 , \ldots , q_n \} </math>
are discrete [[probability distributions]]. Then 

:<math> - \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log p_i \leq - \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log q_i </math>

with equality if and only if
<math> p_i = q_i </math>
for <math>i = 1, \dots n</math>.<ref name="Bremaud2012">{{cite book|author=Pierre Bremaud|title=An Introduction to Probabilistic Modeling|date=6 December 2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4612-1046-7}}</ref>{{rp|68}} Put in words, the [[information entropy]] of a distribution <math>P</math> is less than or equal to its [[cross entropy]] with any other distribution <math>Q</math>.

The difference between the two quantities is the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] or relative entropy, so the inequality can also be written:<ref name="MacKay2003">{{cite book|author=David J. C. MacKay|title=Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms|date=25 September 2003|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-64298-9}}</ref>{{rp|34}}

:<math> D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log \frac{p_i}{q_i} \geq 0.</math>

Note that the use of base-2 [[logarithm]]s is optional, and 
allows one to refer to the quantity on each side of the inequality as an 
"average [[surprisal]]" measured in [[bit]]s.

==Proof==
For simplicity, we prove the statement using the natural logarithm, denoted by {{math|ln}}, since

:<math> \log_b a = \frac{ \ln a }{ \ln b },</math>

so the particular logarithm base {{math|''b'' > 1}} that we choose only scales the relationship by the factor {{math|1 / ln ''b''}}.

Let <math>I</math> denote the set of all <math>i</math> for which ''p<sub>i</sub>'' is non-zero. Then, since <math> \ln x \leq x-1 </math> for all ''x > 0'', with equality if and only if ''x=1'', we have:

:<math>- \sum_{i \in I} p_i \ln \frac{q_i}{p_i} \geq  - \sum_{i \in I} p_i \left( \frac{q_i}{p_i} - 1 \right) </math><math> = - \sum_{i \in I} q_i + \sum_{i \in I} p_i = - \sum_{i \in I} q_i + 1 \geq 0</math>

The last inequality is a consequence of the ''p<sub>i</sub>'' and ''q<sub>i</sub>'' being part of a probability distribution. Specifically, the sum of all non-zero values is 1. Some non-zero ''q<sub>i</sub>'', however, may have been excluded since the choice of indices is conditioned upon the ''p<sub>i</sub>'' being non-zero. Therefore, the sum of the ''q<sub>i</sub>'' may be less than 1.

So far, over the index set  <math>I</math>, we have:

:<math> - \sum_{i \in I} p_i \ln \frac{q_i}{p_i} \geq 0 </math>,

or equivalently
 
:<math> - \sum_{i \in I} p_i \ln q_i \geq - \sum_{i \in I} p_i \ln p_i </math>.

Both sums can be extended to all <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>, i.e. including <math>p_i=0</math>, by recalling that the expression <math>p \ln p</math> tends to 0 as <math>p</math> tends to 0, and <math>(-\ln q)</math> tends to <math>\infty</math> as <math>q</math> tends to 0. We arrive at

:<math> - \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \ln q_i \geq - \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \ln p_i </math>

For equality to hold, we require
# <math> \frac{q_i}{p_i} = 1</math> for all <math>i \in I </math> so that the equality <math>\ln \frac{q_i}{p_i} = \frac{q_i}{p_i} -1 </math> holds, 
# and <math> \sum_{i \in I} q_i = 1</math> which means <math>q_i=0</math> if <math>i\notin I</math>, that is, <math>q_i=0</math> if <math>p_i=0</math>.

This can happen if and only if <math>p_i = q_i </math> for <math>i = 1, \ldots, n</math>.

==Alternative proofs==
The result can alternatively be proved using [[Jensen's inequality]], the [[log sum inequality]], or the fact that the Kullback-Leibler divergence is a form of [[Bregman divergence]]. 

=== Proof by Jensen's inequality ===
Because log is a concave function, we have that:

:<math>\sum_i p_i \log\frac{q_i}{p_i} \le \log\sum_i p_i\frac{q_i}{p_i} = \log\sum_i q_i = 0</math>

where the first inequality is due to Jensen's inequality, and <math>q</math> being a probability distribution implies the last equality.

Furthermore, since <math>\log</math> is strictly concave, by the equality condition of Jensen's inequality we get equality when

:<math>\frac{q_1}{p_1} = \frac{q_2}{p_2} = \cdots = \frac{q_n}{p_n}</math>

and

:<math>\sum_i q_i = 1</math>.

Suppose that this ratio is <math>\sigma</math>, then we have that

:<math>1 = \sum_i q_i = \sum_i \sigma p_i = \sigma</math>

where we use the fact that <math>p, q</math> are probability distributions. Therefore, the equality happens when <math>p = q</math>.

=== Proof by Bregman divergence ===
Alternatively, it can be proved by noting that<math display="block">q - p - p\ln\frac qp \geq 0 </math>for all <math>p, q > 0</math>, with equality holding iff <math>p=q</math>. Then, sum over the states, we have<math display="block">\sum_i q_i - p_i - p_i\ln\frac{q_i}{p_i} \geq 0 </math>with equality holding iff <math>p = q </math>.

This is because the KL divergence is the [[Bregman divergence]] generated by the function <math>t \mapsto \ln t</math>.

==Corollary==
The [[information entropy|entropy]] of <math>P</math> is bounded by:<ref name="Bremaud2012"/>{{rp|68}}

:<math>H(p_1, \ldots , p_n) \leq \log n. </math>

The bound is achieved when <math>q_i = 1/n </math> for all ''i''.
